hints: Look closely at the shape of the leaf in P and Q and where layer X sits. P is flat and open, Q is rolled inwards with X on the inside of the roll.
Remember how bulliform or hinge cells control rolling by gaining and losing water, and link turgid to high (less negative) water potential and flaccid to low (more negative) water potential.
walkthrough:
**Spot what P and Q show**

This is a classic xerophyte response, like marram grass. Layer X is the hinge or bulliform cells on the upper surface.

In P the leaf is flat, so X cells must be swollen with water. In Q the leaf is rolled, so X cells must have lost water and shrunk, pulling the leaf inwards.

**Link water to water potential and turgidity**

Turgid cells have taken up water, so pressure potential is high and overall water potential $\Psi$ is high, that is less negative, close to zero.

Flaccid or plasmolysed cells have lost water, so $\Psi$ is lower, that is more negative. So P has less negative $\Psi$ than Q, and cells can be turgid in P and plasmolysed in Q.

**Check the steady state idea**

Both diagrams show a finished, stable condition, not the moment of change. Water has already moved, so there is now no net diffusion into X in either P or Q.

That makes statements 1, 2 and 4 correct, and statement 3 the opposite of the truth.

options.A: Includes statement 3, which is backwards. Cells are more turgid in flat P than in rolled Q, not less turgid.
options.B: Correctly includes 1, 2 and 4 only. P has less negative water potential and turgid cells, Q has more negative water potential and shrunken cells, with no further net entry in the stable state.
options.C: Misses out statement 2. It is perfectly reasonable that X cells are turgid in P and plasmolysed in Q to cause rolling.
options.D: Includes false statement 3 and misses true statements 1 and 4. P cannot be less turgid than Q if P is the flat, open leaf.
